title: Beyond banks: what non-banks do (and don't do) to monetary policy
source: Bank of England, Bank Underground (Bandera, Bluwstein, Kumhof, Salgado-Moreno, Stevens)
why: A DSGE model estimated on UK data (only 40% of UK corporate debt is now bank lending, down from 60% in 2008) finds that policy-rate transmission is essentially unchanged as non-banks grow, because banks pass rate moves to NBFIs through wholesale funding and NBFIs pass them on through bond markets. QE is different: its effect depends on why non-banks grew, with the output impact of QE 15.4% larger under a firm-driven NBFI expansion, which matters for how central banks read balance-sheet policy as private credit and funds take share.

title: The Surprising Stability of Hedge Fund Repo Haircuts
source: Federal Reserve Board FEDS Notes (Hempel, Kahn, Kurta, Neamtu)
why: Using a new transaction-level series of dealer-to-hedge-fund haircuts in sponsored Treasury repo (November 2019 to September 2026), the authors find that central clearing has not changed haircuts and that haircuts are not procyclical, even under stress. That cuts against a core rationale for the SEC clearing mandate and points stress-amplification worries toward futures margins and dealer intermediation capacity instead, which is directly relevant to basis-trade risk.

title: Looking beyond the baseline: how scenario synthesis helps assess risks
source: ECB Blog (Bańbura, Giannone, Durero, Sun, Zimic)
why: ECB staff show how they weight narrative scenarios (such as the June 2026 Middle East conflict scenarios) against market option-implied, forecaster, and staff risk distributions, treating the weights as relevance to the risk picture, not as probabilities. The worked example shows market-implied euro area inflation risk is far more dispersed and skewed higher than the Survey of Professional Forecasters, a useful window into how the Governing Council reads tail risk around its baseline.

title: Finding Equilibrium Inside the AI Economy
source: Net Interest (Marc Rubinstein; paid post, free preview)
why: From the TomorrowX conference, Rubinstein sets enterprise AI usage claims against Ramp data showing token volume up 27% in four weeks but spending up only 8%, and estimates the US data center buildout (about $9 trillion through 2032) needs roughly $2.7 to $3.5 trillion of annual revenue versus about $108 billion annualized at Anthropic and OpenAI. The paid section argues that lenders rather than demand are now setting the pace of the buildout; the free preview carries the core numbers.

title: When the unthinkable happens: perceptions of monetary policy in tail events
source: BIS Working Paper 1398 (Baumeister, De Fiore, Xiao)
why: The paper shows that after large, rare oil supply shocks, households and firms learning in real time underestimate how hard the central bank responds to inflation, which lifts inflation expectations and produces persistent above-target inflation plus a temporary output overshoot; small shocks barely move beliefs. US nonlinear VAR evidence backs the model, which bears directly on how markets should read a hawkish Fed after this year's Hormuz energy shock.

title: As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking?
source: NY Fed Liberty Street Economics (Boyarchenko, Elias)
why: Boyarchenko and Elias split corporate bond market growth into firms borrowing more overall versus shifting from banks to bonds, finding that 1996-2019 US growth was mostly credit deepening (total nonfinancial corporate credit rose from 41% to 52% of GDP while the bond share only went from 57% to 63%), unlike in other advanced economies. The distinction tells you whether bond-market or bank lending conditions now govern corporate funding, which matters as private credit and bank pullback reshape the credit mix.

title: Why Has Global Trade Remained Resilient Despite High Trade Policy Uncertainty?
source: Federal Reserve Board FEDS Notes (Londono, Ma, Qin)
why: Using 26 countries back to 1960, the note separates news-based trade policy uncertainty from data-based trade flow uncertainty and finds tariff headlines only hurt trade when underlying flows are also hard to predict, which explains why trade kept growing through 2025-26. Ship-tracking data show low-flow-uncertainty countries adjusted after the March 2026 Hormuz disruption by rerouting and front-loading, a useful filter for which trade shocks deserve a macro reaction.

title: The Individual Exception
source: Stratechery (Ben Thompson; free article)
why: Thompson uses Jensen Huang's reinstatement, which added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market cap, to argue that AI is shifting value from managerial bureaucracies to singular individuals, with market cap per employee at the top firms rising steeply since AT&T in the 1950s. It is a framework for why key-person value and headcount deflation may matter more for AI-era valuations than capex totals.

title: Owning the road, not paying the toll: how Europe can keep the returns from AI
source: Bruegel Working Paper 32/2026 (Revoltella, Brasili, Feás)
why: Using Eurostat trade data, the paper maps the AI supply chain in four layers and finds the EU's AI-goods trade balance has swung to a €42 billion deficit, with data-centre infrastructure flipping from a €6 billion surplus in 2015 to an €18 billion deficit in 2025. The one bright spot is chipmaking equipment (ASML, Zeiss), where the surplus grew to €27 billion, which frames where European AI rents are likely to accrue.

title: When Is Monetary Policy Transmission Strongest?
source: San Francisco Fed Economic Letter 2026-34 (Rami Najjar, Adam Shapiro)
why: Using high-frequency FOMC surprises, the authors find that policy shocks pass through to longer-horizon Treasury forward rates mainly when inflation is demand-driven, consistent with the Fed responding about four times more to demand than supply inflation. With supply-driven pressures back, Fed surprises should move the long end less than in past cycles.

title: From Agentic to Agency Risks
source: Citadel Securities Some Macro Thoughts (Nohshad Shah)
why: Shah argues the US is entering a less forgiving phase as fiscal support fades and the Fed leans toward hikes, and uses Ramp data (token spend down 6.3% from its peak while token prices fell 21% in six weeks, with 1% of businesses making up 80% of OpenAI/Anthropic spend) to question AI revenue extrapolation. He adds that political and cyber risk to AI is underpriced and stays defensive on the AI complex, expecting a flatter curve and more pressure on risk assets.

title: The return of inflation: More bank profits, more central bank losses
source: VoxEU/CEPR (Paul De Grauwe, Yuemei Ji)
why: Paying interest on about €2 trillion of reserves means each ECB hike transfers income to banks, lifting euro-area bank ROE toward 10% while the Eurosystem ran €64-69 billion of losses; a 3-4% deposit rate could restore €60-80 billion a year in transfers. The authors argue raising unremunerated minimum reserves from 1% to 2% would cut the subsidy without changing operating procedures.

title: Higher fuel prices seep into core inflation
source: Dallas Fed Economics (Chudik, Kilian, Zhou)
why: Using a structural VAR plus daily-frequency estimators across 149 PCE components, the authors find this year's fuel shock, led by record diesel, added 20 to 60 basis points to 12-month core PCE inflation as of September. If fuel prices simply hold, that contribution fades by about 30 basis points by end-2027, a useful anchor for how much of sticky core is energy pass-through versus something the Fed has to fight.

title: Anthropic's compute spending is increasing by 4x per year, outpacing OpenAI's 3x
source: Epoch AI Data Insight (Josh You)
why: Using Anthropic's S-1/A, Epoch shows compute and infrastructure spend rising from $433 million in 2023 to nearly $10 billion in Q3 2026 (about $40 billion annualized), versus roughly 3x a year at OpenAI. It also flags $447.5 billion of contracted compute commitments through 2030, only about another doubling from today's run rate, which suggests the 4x pace has to slow and matters for whoever is financing the capacity.

title: Financial Stability Review, November 2026
source: European Central Bank (Financial Stability Review)
why: The ECB's twice-yearly risk map says AI valuations rest on very ambitious earnings expectations while AI firms keep adding debt and circular financing makes real demand hard to gauge, with banks exposed mainly through their links to non-banks. Skip to Box 3 (debt financing of AI), Box 4 (big tech in the euro bond market), Box 6 (synthetic risk transfers) and Box 7 (hedge funds in sovereign repo) for the parts that matter most to AI credit and positioning; the full report is long.

title: Clouds of Credit: Mapping the Financial Web Behind AI Compute
source: NBER Working Paper 36032 (Van Nieuwerburgh, Su)
why: Maps the network of debt, leases and non-recourse project finance behind the AI compute buildout and calibrates a model in which debt funds nearly 60% of the coming expansion and firms overinvest relative to the social optimum. In a low-productivity state losses reach $16.8 trillion with 40% loss-given-default on debt, and contractual spillovers among the key firms account for about 30% of private losses; read the abstract and the network section if short on time.

title: Explaining the stock market: Why is it still so hard?
source: VoxEU/CEPR (Bryan Kelly, Yinan Su, Chao Zhang)
why: Using an LLM to pull the stated reasons out of one Wall Street Journal market recap per trading day (2002 to 2024), the authors explain about 30% of daily and 40% of monthly S&P 500 return variation out of sample, against roughly 10% at best for macro, cash-flow, expectations and flow benchmarks. Corporate news, macro activity and sentiment each explain 6 to 9% of daily variation, and anticipated reasons outperform random subsets, which cuts against the idea that the recaps are just after-the-fact storytelling.

title: How Hedge Funds Are Navigating Stock Market Volatility
source: Goldman Sachs, The Markets (Vincent Lin, Prime Insights and Analytics)
why: Goldman prime book data show five straight weeks of hedge fund degrossing, then a shift to adding hedges last week, with ETF shorts up about 19 percentage points, the third-largest weekly increase in a decade; fast money (hedge funds, CTAs) sits near multi-year-low positioning while ETFs and mutual funds took in about $150 billion during the drawdown. Fundamental long/short funds are still up about 7% after peaking near 17% at midyear, and the desk reads the market as "buyers live higher" into year-end; the closing trade ideas are opinion, the flow numbers are the reason to read it.

title: Canada's monetary policy framework: A trusted anchor in uncertain waters
source: Bank of Canada (Governor Tiff Macklem, speech)
why: Macklem lays out the conclusions of the 2027 to 2031 framework renewal: total CPI stays the target, the Bank will lean on CPI-trim and CPIX as its two main core gauges, and it admits it was too slow to see how persistent and broad post-pandemic inflation was. He frames today as a live supply-shock test, with inflation near 3% since April, businesses so far absorbing energy costs but more pass-through expected, which is why the Bank hiked 25 basis points to 2.5% in October.

title: Policy driven trade imbalances: The case of sovereign wealth funds
source: PIIE RealTime Economics (Joseph E. Gagnon, Nishtha Agrawal)
why: Their estimates say each $1 of fiscal surplus raises the trade balance by about $0.30 and each $1 of official foreign-asset purchases by about $0.50, or $0.80 or more when combined. Across 12 major oil exporters, persistent surpluses show up only where governments park oil revenue abroad through sovereign wealth funds (Norway, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia), which makes official flows, not commodity luck, the variable to watch for global imbalances.

title: Five Facts About Stablecoins
source: NBER Working Paper 36038 (Cong, Liao, Prasad, Zhang)
why: Wallet-level blockchain data for 2020 to 2025 show stablecoins working as a transaction currency, with on-chain volume above Bitcoin, rising velocity and a shift toward small transfers, plus falling wallet access costs since 2023 and growing use as the settlement asset of on-chain credit that seems to reallocate rather than destroy credit. Smart contracts touch about a third of Ethereum stablecoin transactions and over two thirds of volume; note that co-author Gordon Liao is Circle's chief economist, and the abstract plus the five fact sections are the efficient read.
